newsitem.title: USA: Bill's delay could save millions on pro stadium costs.
newsitem.headline: Bill's delay could save millions on pro stadium costs.

text.p: Cities planning to build new professional sports stadiums stand to save millions of dollars following a decision last week by a key senator to delay legislation affecting stadium financing.

According to a congressional source, Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, D-N.Y., probably will delay the effective date of a bill he introduced in June to bar use of tax-exempt bonds for construction of professional sports stadiums.
In the past, state and local officials involved in stadium financings have relied heavily on tax-exempt bonds, which allow them to borrow money at significantly lower interest rates.
The expected delay in Moynihan's June 14, 1996, effective date means big savings for a number of cities nationwide with major facilities on the drawing board, bond market sources said.
There is going to be a "huge sigh of relief," Robert Durante, director of surveillance for Standard & Poor's Rating Services, said in a telephone interview Monday.

The congressional source familiar with the legislation, who asked not to be identified, said Moynihan will likely delay the effective date of the bill to sometime in January, when the Senator plans to reintroduce the measure.
The bill was was not acted on this session.
"There are a lot of deals that are going on right now that are going to save a significant amount of money" as a result of the delay in the effective date, Durante said.
He pointed, for instance, to Cincinnati, which has major, high-tech football and baseball stadiums totalling $540 million in the works.
If Cincinnati had to issue taxable instead of tax-exempt bonds for the mega-facilities, it would have to shell out an extra $200 million, the analyst estimated.

Moynihan aides have not announced that the senator plans to revise the effective date. John Talisman, chief tax counsel for Moynihan on the Senate Finance Committee, said he had no comment on the report of the delay.
But the congressional source said, "We're not sure what the date is going to be, but it won't be June 14, 1996. If it gets changed, anything that's going on now will be exempted."
The congressional source said the bill is needed to "correct the law," not to hurt municipalities. "We're not trying to be bad guys here."
A bond market spokesman called the upcoming delay in the effective date "important and encouraging."
"It is an extremely helpful sign to the marketplace that projects currently underway can move forward," said Micah Green, executive vice president of the Public Securities Association trade group.
But Green said the PSA hopes Moynihan takes his plan to ease the bill's effective date one step further by changing it to the date any bill actually clears Congress.
